The reference row: how the URL answered before the migration.

The URL already fails on the reference, so there is nothing to compare. It is listed in the sitemap search engines know, though. Possible causes: a detail page (news, job offer, product) listed in the page sitemap that only works with a record in its URL; an error in a plugin or content element; a page for logged-in users only.
Same path, same page or record.
The URL redirects to the same page or record. Nothing to do, unless a warning says otherwise.

The URL leads to the same page or record, but not in one step: the redirect points at a URL that redirects again, or at a page that names another URL as canonical. Point the redirect directly at the suggested final URL.

The URL answers with an error on the target and does not redirect. Possible causes: the page was moved or renamed without a redirect; it was not migrated, is hidden or not translated; its slug changed; an error on the target itself — check the status code.

The URL redirects, but ends in an error, a loop or too many redirects. Possible causes: the redirect target was deleted or moved; redirect rules lead into each other; rules for https, www or a trailing slash undo each other.

The URL answers with 200, but shows a different page, record or language. Possible causes: a redirect to a parent or start page; the slug is used by another page now; a language fallback shows the default language.

The URL answers with 200, but the markers needed for a comparison are missing. Possible causes: one environment does not render the page uid in the body tag or the record meta tag; a page template replaces the body tag.
A page from the target sitemap, requested to suggest redirect targets.
No complete answer within the timeout, also after the retries. The page may exist and only render slowly, e.g. right after a cache flush. Run the check again before treating it as missing.

The URL calls a page that shows content only with a parameter — the detail page of a plugin — without one. Whatever it answers, there is no page of its own to keep: the detail views are checked one by one. The page is marked in its page properties.

Possible causes: a detail page listed in the page sitemap that needs a record in its URL — the plugin fails without one; an exception in a plugin or content element; a database or configuration error on this environment. The TYPO3 log of this environment names the exception.
Possible causes: the page was moved or renamed without a redirect; it is hidden, deleted or not translated; the record of a detail page no longer exists.
Possible causes: the page is restricted to logged-in users; Basic Auth for this environment is missing or wrong; a web server rule blocks the request.
The server refused the request. Possible causes: a web server or firewall rule, rate limiting, or arguments in the URL the site does not accept.
The request got no HTTP answer. Possible causes: the host is unreachable, a DNS or certificate error, or a timeout — a higher --timeout may help.
More than one redirect before the final page. Point the first redirect directly at the final URL.
The chain contains a 302, 303 or 307. A permanent move should answer 301 or 308.
A deep URL redirects to a start page. Search engines often treat this as a soft 404.
The sitemap lists a URL that redirects. A sitemap should only contain final URLs.
The target page is in a different language than the reference page.
Several URLs render this page without a record marker — probably a detail page. Which record is shown cannot be compared.
The same record is rendered by more than one page. That is duplicate content.
A redirect leads to a TYPO3 shortcut page, which redirects again with 307. Point the redirect at the target of the shortcut.
The redirect ends on a page that names another URL as canonical — typically a page that shows the content of another page. Point the redirect at the canonical URL.
The sitemap lists a URL whose page names another URL as canonical. A sitemap should only contain canonical URLs.
The sitemap lists a page that shows content only with a parameter, called without one. Exclude it from the page sitemap.

The same page renders records under other URLs. If it shows content only with a record, this URL is a detail page without one and does not belong in the sitemap; if it shows a list as well, nothing is wrong.

A snapshot stores the sitemaps of every language of a site at one point in time, raw XML included. It is the URL list every check works with, and it stays available after the site itself has changed.
Choose a base URL of a configured site and find its sitemaps. The environment is suggested from the site configuration.
Select the languages, give the snapshot a label if you like, and import it.
Lock every snapshot you must not lose, e.g. the live state before a relaunch: the lock icon protects it from deletion, also by the cleanup command.
URLs outside the configured sites and scheduled imports need the command line: websitecheck:importsitemaps. Before the database is replaced, save the snapshots you need as files below.

Checks whether every URL of a sitemap snapshot works: the HTTP status and TYPO3 error pages per URL. The link check also follows the plugin links on those pages, which no sitemap lists, and reports links whose arguments have no effect.
Import a sitemap snapshot of the environment to check in the Sitemaps module.
Compose the check below and run the command on the command line. Every URL is requested, which can take a while.
Reload this page and review the results: filter by environment and problems, mark findings as reviewed and add a note where needed.
Moved URLs and redirects are the job of the migration check: it compares two environments page by page.
Checks whether the URLs search engines know from the old site still lead to the same page or record on the new one — directly or through a redirect.
Before the switch: import the sitemaps of the live site and lock the snapshot.
Import a snapshot of the new site, e.g. staging, compose the check below and run it. Repeat after every change to the new site.
Review the results: missing redirects per page and record, with a suggested target where one can be derived.

After the switch: import a snapshot of the new live site and reuse the reference results of the last run — the old site no longer answers. Export the last run beforehand if the database gets replaced.
Both sites have to render the page and record markers described in the documentation; without them pages cannot be compared.

Requests the paths of the snapshot on another host. Example: the snapshot was taken on www.example.com, the host is staging.example.com — you see before the switch whether every URL search engines know answers on the new system. Or the other way round: a sitemap provider only exists on staging while the pages are live already. Redirects and content are compared by the migration check.

Results are stored per environment label and URL; a new run with the same label replaces them. Use one label per environment and check, e.g. "staging" for the status check and "staging-links" for the link check of the same site.

A shape is the path of a link plus the names of its arguments. /news/detail?tx_news_pi1[news]=12 and …[news]=13 share one shape, so a list of a hundred news items is checked with this many links, not a hundred.
The URLs of the old site as search engines know them. Take the locked live snapshot from before the switch — a newer live snapshot already lists the URLs of the new site.

Before the switch, both sites answer and every run requests both. After it, www.example.com shows the new site: a run named "relaunch" from before the switch still knows how every old URL answered, and a run "after-relaunch" reuses those rows and only requests the new site.
They name the two sides in the results, e.g. "live" and "staging". After the switch both are live: "live-before" and "live-after" keep them apart.
Says where the snapshot comes from. The migration check suggests the locked live snapshot as reference and the newest staging, development or local one as target — so tag live snapshots as live.
The name the checks use to find the snapshot, e.g. "live-before-relaunch". It has to be unique. Left empty, it is the host and the time, e.g. "www.example.com 2026-01-31 14:05".

A database that is replaced — e.g. by a fresh import of the live database — takes every snapshot and every stored check result with it. A saved file brings them back, and it moves them to another installation, e.g. from staging to the new live system. The files are the same as those of websitecheck:exportsnapshots.
